Meeting header: 2028-01-17 15:00 UTC, Duration ~72 mins. Attendees listed above.

[00:00:00] Jasmine (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for blocking time. Quick intro from Redwood side, I'm Jasmine, AE, and Marco here is our performance SE.
[00:00:08] Marco (SE): Hi all. We're excited to walk through the traces you sent and talk about the kernel-level differences we've been seeing between TRTL and vLLM builds.
[00:00:16] Samir (Orchid): Thanks. We have a noisy production workload—mixed real-time chat and batch re-ranks—and latency variance is killing SLO compliance. We also run inside a VPC-connected on-prem cluster, so networked storage and NVLink topologies are slightly odd.
[00:00:29] Marco: Got it. Before we dig in, can you confirm the model family and quantization you tested? The CSV you attached had a 4-bit column but not clear if it's Q4_0 or Q4_K_M.
[00:00:44] Lena (Orchid): We used what our packaging script called q4_k on the TRTL side and q4_o on vLLM, I think. There might be a mismatch. The packaging is... sorry the packaging was a bit ad hoc.
[00:00:51] Marco: Okay that's helpful — small differences in quant mapping can change kernel selection dramatically.
[00:01:05] [00:01:05] Discussion: Kernel warmup and persistent KV cache
[00:01:05] Marco: One pattern we saw in your traces: TRTL prefers fused multi-head attention kernels for the 2-16 token window, whereas vLLM's PyTorch path picks a generic matmul-attn pipeline which causes more small-kernel launches. That mismatch combined with CUDA Graph replay creates a tail latency spike.
[00:01:21] Samir: Right, we see intermittent 200-400ms spikes on requests that should be 40-60ms. The spikes correlate with CUDA Graph replay attempts in the NVTX logs.
[00:01:33] Marco: Two causes: (1) Graph capture boundaries sometimes capture different kernel sequences when KV cache priming is happening, so replay doesn't match runtime and falls back to non-graph execution. (2) If your persistent KV cache eviction is thrashing memory banks, kernels will serialize on memory ops.
[00:01:47] Tanya (Orchid): We do see eviction churn during larger fanouts. Is there a recommended eviction policy?
[00:01:53] Marco: For on-prem with limited GPU RAM, set a heuristic: keep prefix cache for conversational sessions up to 256 tokens pinned and evict older contexts. Also tune the allocator to use a best-fit decreasing strategy rather than naive LRU—this reduces fragmentation and kernel stalls.
[00:02:08] [00:02:08] Transcription note: 'best-fit' sounded like 'best-fit decreasing' in the recording; may be slightly off.
[00:02:18] [00:02:18] Discussion: CUDA Graphs and non-deterministic replays
[00:02:18] Marco: CUDA Graphs give great throughput but are brittle when control flow changes. If your batch size or sequence length distribution deviates at capture time, graphs can either error or silently record suboptimal kernel order. We recommend: record multiple graph variants keyed by (max_seq, batch, quant_profile) and have runtime tiebreakers.
[00:02:34] Lena: That's what we suspected. Right now we only capture one graph per model and hope for the best.
[00:02:40] Marco: That explains it. Also TRTL's fused kernels are more sensitive to alignment—if tokens align to certain warp widths, TRTL will select fused attention. vLLM's path is conservative and will launch smaller block kernels which are more stable but higher overhead per call.
[00:02:55] [00:02:55] Discussion: Quantization mismatches
[00:02:55] Marco: The q4_k / q4_o mismatch you mentioned earlier causes different dequantization kernels. TRTL has optimized int8/deq-paths that avoid a separate kernel step in some conversions; vLLM's dequant tends to be a separate pass. At scale that's extra kernel overhead.
[00:03:10] Samir: So we should normalize quant formats before benching?
[00:03:13] Marco: Exactly. Also flag the quant profile in the graph key so you don't capture a graph with q4_k but replay with q4_o.
[00:03:20] [00:03:20] Discussion: NVLink / NUMA and memory bank affinity
[00:03:20] Marco: On your topology, NVLink segments pair some GPUs with asymmetric bandwidth. That can surface as long tail if the runtime migrates KV cache between banks. Pin KV allocations to GPU-local memory and avoid cross-node migrations unless the pipeline explicitly needs it.
[00:03:36] Tanya: Do we need to re-architect our placement driver? Right now it balances by load, not affinity.
[00:03:42] Jasmine: For production we'd recommend affinity-first with a soft-balancer—evict only when utilization crosses a higher threshold. That often reduces cross-GPU memcpy spikes.
[00:03:54] [00:03:54] Discussion: Batching strategy and SLOs
[00:03:54] Marco: You mentioned mixed real-time plus batch. There's a policy we use: separate 'latency lanes' and 'throughput lanes'. Latency lane uses small batch sizes, no graph capture, and low-latency kernels; throughput lane uses larger batches with CUDA Graphs and fused kernels. Route by policy at request ingress.
[00:04:10] Samir: What's the break-even batch size for TRTL fused kernels vs vLLM?
[00:04:15] Marco: In our microbench it sits around batch 8-12 for 1-2 token outputs on A100-like hardware. For longer seqs (64+ tokens) the fused path often wins earlier. But this is topology and quant-dependent. We'll send you the sheet with curves.
[00:04:29] [00:04:29] Interruption / crosstalk
[00:04:29] Ben (Security): Quick interjection on encryption—how do we handle KMS unwrap during runtime? Does the KV cache keep plaintext?
[00:04:37] Marco: Good question. Best practice: KV cache should be resident in GPU memory and not stored in plaintext on host; decryption should happen in a secure enclave or at process start and keys kept in GPU-resident buffers when supported. If that's not possible, you need an HSM-backed decrypt and frequent rewrap.
[00:04:53] Ben: We'll send a list of requirements.
[00:04:56] [00:04:56] Deep dive: Tracing artifacts and NVTX examples
[00:04:56] Marco: We pulled the NVTX you uploaded. I annotated three spans where kernel choice flips: at step 12, 27, and 38 in the trace. The pattern: capture->replay mismatch, then fallback to cuLaunchKernel path which costs 120ms on your infra.
[00:05:12] Marco: I'll attach a short NVTX snippet you can drop into your runner. It includes a reproducible script to capture a graph with primed KV cache and replay it with synthetic session traffic.
[00:05:25] Lena: That'd be great. Our ops people can run it during the maintenance window.
[00:05:29] [00:05:29] Practical mitigation steps discussed
[00:05:29] Marco: Short term: pinness, multiple graph variants keyed by (seq_len, batch, quant), increase graph-capture determinism by ensuring a primed KV cache before capture, and a fallback 'fast path' policy that rejects graph replay and falls back to pre-warmed kernels rather than naive replay.
[00:05:44] Samir: For the fallback, do you have code examples?
[00:05:47] Marco: Yes — we'll include a snippet in the runbook. It basically tests graph validity against a small sanity tensor and if mismatch occurs it uses an alternative kernel path with no capture.
[00:05:58] [00:05:58] Discussion: vLLM's scheduler vs TRTL's kernel mapper
[00:05:58] Marco: Another distinction: vLLM tends to schedule more fine-grained CUDA streams which exposes concurrency but also increases small kernel overhead. TRTL's mapper tries to fuse multiple ops into bigger kernels, reducing launches but increasing memory pressure. For constrained GPU RAM, vLLM might be more stable.
[00:06:15] Tanya: So we pick the runtime per lane based on memory headroom?
[00:06:18] Marco: Exactly — throughput lane prefers TRTL fused kernels with larger memory headroom; latency lane might use vLLM or a TRTL config that disables certain fusions.
[00:06:26] [00:06:26] Anecdote / imperfect transcription
[00:06:26] Marco: (inaudible) — we had one customer where enabling fusion reduced tokens/sec by 15% because of bank thrashing, so the metric to watch is not just latency but tail and tokens/sec.
[00:06:40] [00:06:40] Security and compliance notes
[00:06:40] Ben: On the SOC2 front: we need audit logs for model version changes and who triggered graph captures. Is that supported?
[00:06:47] Jasmine: Redwood can emit audit events for graph capture, model rollout, and config changes; we can forward to your SIEM. We'll attach the docs.
[00:06:55] Ben: Also SSO / SAML integration for the on-prem console?
[00:06:58] Jasmine: Yep, SAML + RBAC is supported in Private. We'll include the integration guide.
[00:07:06] [00:07:06] Wrap-up and recap
[00:07:06] Jasmine: To recap: main suspects for your spikes are CUDA Graph capture/replay mismatches, quant-format disparities, and NVLink/NUMA affinity causing KV thrash. Short term: run the NVTX replay script, pin KV caches where possible, and capture multiple graph variants. Medium term: set up a two-lane routing policy and a pilot with Redwood to test TRTL and vLLM lanes side-by-side on your cluster.
[00:07:26] Samir: That sounds good. We'll coordinate with Marco on the exact pilot window.
[00:07:30] Jasmine: Great. I'll send the spreadsheet and the runbook after this call. Any last questions?
[00:07:36] Lena: None from me.
[00:07:38] Ben: I'll forward compliance items.
[00:07:40] Marcus (SE offhand): Thanks everyone.
[00:07:44] Jasmine: Thanks all — talk soon.
